What 'Family Flowers Only' Means on a Funeral Notice

You have read the notice, you want to do something, and one line has stopped you: family flowers only.

It is a short phrase and it is easy to read it as a door closing. It is not meant that way. It is a practical request, made by people who are organising a service in a short window of time, and it is asking you to do something other than send an arrangement.

This guide explains what the phrase means, why families use it, what to send in its place, and how to word it if you are the one writing the notice.

What 'family flowers only' means

The meaning is narrow and literal. Only the immediate family will be arranging floral tributes for the service. Everyone else is asked not to send one.

It is not a comment on how close you were to the person who died, and it is not a test. It applies to colleagues, neighbours, old school friends and extended family alike. If the notice says it, the family has already decided what will be at the service, and your arrangement would arrive outside that decision.

The wording on Australian notices varies, and the differences matter:

Wording on the notice
What it is asking of you
Family flowers onlyDo not send a tribute. The family is handling what appears at the service
Family flowers only, donations to [charity]As above, with a named place to direct the gesture instead
No flowers by requestNobody is sending tributes, the family included
In lieu of flowers, donations to [charity]A donation is the preferred gesture rather than an arrangement
Donations preferredSofter. A tribute is not ruled out, but a donation is what they would rather receive
Floral tributes welcomeSend one if you would like to

If you are unsure which of these you are reading, the funeral director handling the service will tell you, and they are used to the question.

Why a family asks for it

Almost always for a practical reason rather than a sentimental one.

  • The space is small. A chapel service, a graveside, or a service at a private home does not hold thirty arrangements, and a crowded space is harder for the family to move through on a hard day.
  • They want the gesture to go somewhere else. A named charity, a hospice, or research into the illness the person died from. This is the most common reason by a distance.
  • Someone would have to deal with them afterwards. Tributes are not usually kept after the service, and the family has to decide what happens to each one within a day or two of the funeral.
  • Allergies or health reasons. Strongly scented arrangements are difficult in a closed chapel, and some aged care and hospital chapels restrict them.
  • Cultural or religious practice. Some traditions do not include floral tributes, or restrict them to specific forms and colours.
  • Cost and distance. Families often know that people will spend money they do not have, or send from interstate at short notice, and would rather spare them that.

None of these reasons is about you, which is worth remembering if the phrase has left you feeling awkward.

What to send instead

The request removes one option. It does not remove the gesture.

  1. Give to the charity named in the notice. Most funeral directors run a donation page for the service, and many charities will tell the family who gave, without the amount. If no charity is named, one connected to the illness or to something the person cared about is always appropriate.
  2. Write properly. A card with two or three specific sentences about the person is kept, read again months later, and valued far more than most people expect. Say the thing you actually remember.
  3. Send food. A meal that can go straight in the freezer, delivered in the week after the service rather than the day of it, when the house has gone quiet.
  4. Offer something concrete. School pick-ups, a lift to the service, mowing, a week of dog walks. Name the thing and the day rather than asking them to think of something.
  5. Mark it later. A tree, a plant for the garden, or a single arrangement sent to the home a month on, when the cards have stopped arriving. This is often the one that lands hardest, in the best way.

If you want to send something and the notice has named a charity, give to the charity. That is the request, in plain terms.

When sending something is still fine

There are a few situations where the request does not apply to you.

You are immediate family. The phrase exists to describe what you are doing, so if you are a partner, child, parent or sibling, you are inside it and you are likely the person arranging the funeral florals for the service.

The service has already happened. The request covers the funeral itself. Something sent to the home in the weeks afterwards sits outside it, and often arrives at a better moment.

The wording was softer than you first read. Donations preferred is a preference, not an instruction. Floral tributes welcome is an invitation.

You have asked and been told it is fine. If you are close enough to the family to ask directly, ask. A short message saying you would like to send something and will do whatever they prefer is never unwelcome.

Outside those, take the notice at its word.

If you are the one writing the notice

Be specific, and give people somewhere to put the feeling. A request with no alternative reads as a refusal, and people will send something anyway because they need to do something.

What works:

  • Name the charity, and give the donation link or the funeral director's page where it can be made
  • Keep it to one line, placed at the end of the notice where people expect it
  • Say family flowers only rather than no flowers if your own tribute will be at the service, so nobody is confused by what they see on the day
  • Tell the funeral director what you have asked for, so they can answer calls on your behalf

What it will not do: stop everyone. Some arrangements will arrive regardless, usually from people who did not see the notice. The funeral director will handle them, and there is no need for you to deal with it on the day. That is not a failure of the wording, and most families find the ones that do arrive are a comfort rather than an imposition. Deciding what the family's own funeral florals will be is a separate decision, and usually an easier one once the notice is settled.

What the family usually arranges

In most Australian services it comes down to three pieces. The main tribute that sits on the coffin, one or two smaller pieces from children or grandchildren, and something for the entrance or the memorial table beside the photograph. A graveside or a wake may add one more.

The timing is tighter than people expect. Services are commonly held three to seven days after the death, and the funeral director will usually want everything delivered to the chapel sixty to ninety minutes before the service starts. That leaves a short window for design and sourcing, which is why this is one conversation worth having early rather than in the last two days.

What helps a designer most is not a flower name. It is the person. Their garden, the colours they wore, whether they would have hated something formal, whether natives feel more like them than roses. That is enough to build a tribute that looks like it belongs to them.
